children.text: Proposals for a portfolio office meet the same objections in almost every public organization. Chapter 15 anticipates five and answers each. This lesson works through them, then turns to the implementation roadmap the book schedules backward from the January 2028 deadline, and ends with the single question the book recommends to legislators and board members who oversee a transformation.
Knowing the objections in advance matters because each contains a partial truth. A good answer acknowledges what is right in the objection before explaining why the conclusion does not follow.
The objections are written for Vermont, but each has an equivalent in a hospital boardroom or another state's agency, and the answers transfer with them.
Objections One and Two: 'We Already Manage This' and 'This Is Government'

The first objection is that existing arrangements already cover the work: the Health Care Advisory Committee and monthly reports. The partial truth is that these provide real oversight. The book's answer is that the HCAC is a governance body, not a portfolio office. It provides oversight, not an integrated master schedule, resource-conflict resolution, a maintained risk register or earned-value tracking, and the monthly reports track activities rather than performance. The HCAC is the right governance body; it needs a portfolio office to give it the data to govern.

The second objection is that government does not run projects like the private sector. The partial truth is that public programs have different accountabilities. The book's answer is that Vermont's transformation is a time-bounded, outcome-specified, heavily financed portfolio of interdependent programs with legally binding deadlines. The Rural Health Transformation Program is a federal cooperative agreement with deliverables and reporting obligations; the withdrawn AHEAD agreement still carries federal closeout requirements; Act 68 has a statutory deliverable in January 2028. Federal partners expect professional management of exactly this kind of work.

Both answers share a pattern: they accept the premise and show that it does not reach the conclusion. Yes, there is oversight; no, oversight is not management. Yes, this is government; that is precisely why its obligations demand professional delivery.
Oversight asks whether the work is going well. Management makes it go well. A portfolio needs both, and one cannot substitute for the other.
Objections Three, Four and Five: Cost, Hospitals and Consultants

The third objection is cost in a year of budget cuts. Lesson 13 gave the full answer: Rural Health Transformation Program funds depend on demonstrated progress, the office costs a small fraction of the value it protects, and the alternative is a partial transformation that costs far more. The fourth is that hospitals will not accept being managed by AHS. The book's answer clarifies the role: the Portfolio Manager does not manage hospitals but manages AHS's contribution to the portfolio. Hospital plans are produced by hospitals, approved by AHS and monitored through the Green Mountain Care Board.

The fifth objection is the newest: AHS already has expert help. Its March 2026 Act 68 report lists contracted support from Manatt, Phelps & Phillips, a new hospital technical-assistance vendor and analytics support under negotiation. The book's answer is that a contractor delivers a defined scope. It cannot hold a state component back until its upstream gate opens, reassign agency staff between components, or answer to the Legislature for the portfolio as a whole. Contracted support adds capacity, not authority, and every new contract is another component that someone has to sequence.

Taken together, the five answers define the role by contrast. It is not oversight, not a private-sector import, not an unaffordable luxury, not control over hospitals and not something a contractor can supply. It is the integrating authority that none of the existing arrangements provides.

children.text: The Implementation Roadmap

The book anchors its roadmap to the one date that cannot move: the Statewide Strategic Plan, due January 15, 2028. Figure 15.10 schedules the portfolio office's build-out backward from that deadline and against the components it exists to sequence. A Portfolio Manager hired by January 2027 has nine months before FY2028 hospital budgets take effect in October 2027, which the book judges enough only if the office is running before the Technology gate it is meant to protect.

From mid-2027 the office runs on a fixed cadence: monthly governance reviews, quarterly performance reviews against the Vermont Scorecard, and annual portfolio rebalancing. The book's aim is that the January 2028 plan arrives with portfolio-management evidence, benefits tracked, risks managed and resources deployed in dependency order, after which the office carries the portfolio into the plan's three-year update cycle.

Scheduling backward from a fixed deadline is itself a portfolio technique. It exposes how little time remains for each step and makes the cost of delay concrete: every month the portfolio office is late is a month of gating decisions made without it.

children.text: The Question Oversight Should Ask

Chapter 15's advice to legislators and board members is a single question that separates a real portfolio from a reporting exercise: which component is currently the binding constraint on all the others, who owns it, and what would it take to accelerate it? An organization managing a genuine portfolio can answer in one sentence. An organization managing a list will answer with a status summary of all nineteen components.

The question works because it can only be answered by someone who sees the dependencies. Identifying the binding constraint requires knowing which upstream work is holding back the most downstream value. Naming its owner requires that ownership be assigned. Saying what would accelerate it requires having thought about resources across components. A reporting function cannot answer it; a portfolio function answers it routinely.

Oversight bodies can ask the question at every review and track whether the answer changes. If the binding constraint never moves, either the portfolio is not acting on it or the answer is not being given honestly. Both are findings an oversight body should want to know.
Which component is currently the binding constraint on all the others, who owns it, and what would it take to accelerate it? (Transforming Healthcare, Chapter 15)
Preparing for the Objections in Your Own Setting

Before proposing a portfolio function, write down the objections you expect, in the words your organization will use. In a hospital they may be that the executive team already coordinates, that service-line leaders own their own changes, or that the transformation office would duplicate finance and quality. Each usually maps to one of the book's five.

For each, prepare the partial truth and the answer, with evidence from your own inventory, sequencing results, risk register and benefits trace. Objections are answered most convincingly not by argument about governance but by showing a specific dependency nobody owns, a specific risk nobody manages, or a specific component running ahead of its gate.

Finally, prepare your own answer to the oversight question. If you cannot yet say which component is your portfolio's binding constraint, who owns it and what would accelerate it, that inability is the strongest argument for the function you are proposing.
The most persuasive answer to any objection is a concrete example from your own portfolio: an unowned dependency, an unmanaged cross-pillar risk, or a component running ahead of its gate.

points: Chapter 15 answers five objections: existing governance, government is different, cost, hospital acceptance and existing consultants.
The HCAC is a governance body; oversight is not management, and it needs a portfolio office to supply the data it governs with.
The Portfolio Manager manages AHS's contribution to the portfolio, not the hospitals, whose plans are approved by AHS and monitored through the GMCB.
Contractors add capacity, not authority; they cannot hold components back, reassign staff or answer for the whole portfolio.
The roadmap is scheduled backward from January 15, 2028: Portfolio Manager by January 2027, office operational by Q2 2027, before FY2028 budgets in October 2027.
From mid-2027 the office runs monthly governance, quarterly Scorecard reviews and annual rebalancing.
The oversight question is which component is the binding constraint, who owns it and what would accelerate it; a real portfolio answers in one sentence.

A status summary of every component is the characteristic answer of an organization managing a list.
